title: Acceptance of artificial intelligence among pre-service teachers: a multigroup analysis
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines what drives pre-service teachers’ acceptance of AI-based educational applications and whether those drivers differ by gender. The study is framed around the Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3) and asks which factors predict behavioral intention to use AI in education, with particular attention to AI self-efficacy, perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, job relevance, and subjective norm.

The study did not evaluate a specific AI product or instructional intervention. Instead, it used a survey of 452 pre-service teachers enrolled at one German university in teacher education programs, collecting self-reported perceptions of AI use in education. Analyses included confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, measurement invariance testing, latent mean comparisons, and multigroup analysis by gender.

Results showed that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use were the strongest predictors of intention to use AI, with AI self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment also contributing indirectly through perceived ease of use. AI anxiety did not significantly predict perceived ease of use in the overall model, although gender moderated some relationships: female pre-service teachers showed higher AI anxiety, and the path from AI anxiety to perceived ease of use differed by gender. The authors conclude that AI acceptance in teacher education depends mainly on perceived usefulness and ease of use, and that training programs should address gender-specific concerns and provide better preparation for AI-supported teaching.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical correlational study using survey data, SEM, and multigroup invariance analysis, but it does not evaluate an instructional intervention or learning outcomes. It is useful for understanding acceptance determinants, yet it provides only indirect evidence for educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct evidence of achievement or other student outcome effects; it measures intentions, perceptions, and gender differences in AI acceptance among pre-service teachers. Any impact on K-12 learning is speculative and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based acceptance of AI-based educational applications among pre-service teachers, including general AI tools and references to AI-powered educational products such as chatbots, learning analytics, recommendations, diagnostics, and adaptive learning applications; no specific classroom intervention was implemented.
